## Proof

**Notation.** Let $\log_1 n = \log n$, $\log_2 n = \log\log n$, and in general $\log_{i+1} n = \log(\log_i n)$. Choose $N$ large enough that all iterated logarithms $\log_1 n, \dots, \log_{j+1} n$ are defined and exceed $1$ for $n \ge N$. The series in question is

$$S_j(p) \;=\; \sum_{n=N}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\,n\,\log_1 n\,\log_2 n\,\cdots\,\log_j n\,(\log_{j+1} n)^p\,}.$$

**Claim.** $S_j(p)$ converges if and only if $p > 1$.

We prove this by induction on $j \ge 0$, using the **Cauchy condensation test**: if $f$ is nonnegative and eventually decreasing, then $\sum f(n)$ converges iff $\sum 2^k f(2^k)$ converges.

The general term $f(n) = \dfrac{1}{n\,\log_1 n\,\cdots\,\log_j n\,(\log_{j+1}n)^p}$ is eventually decreasing (its denominator is eventually increasing in $n$), so condensation applies.

---

**Base case $j = 0$.** The product $\log_1\cdots\log_j$ is empty, so

$$S_0(p) = \sum_{n=N}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n\,(\log n)^p}.$$

Condensation gives the comparison series

$$\sum_{k} 2^k \cdot \frac{1}{2^k\,(\log 2^k)^p} = \sum_{k} \frac{1}{(k\log 2)^p} = \frac{1}{(\log 2)^p}\sum_{k}\frac{1}{k^p},$$

which converges iff $p > 1$. Hence $S_0(p)$ converges iff $p>1$. ✓

---

**Inductive step.** Suppose the claim holds for $j-1$ (with $j \ge 1$). Apply condensation to $S_j(p)$:

$$\sum_{k} 2^k f(2^k) = \sum_{k} \frac{1}{\log_1(2^k)\,\log_2(2^k)\,\cdots\,\log_j(2^k)\,(\log_{j+1}(2^k))^p}.$$

Now examine each factor. We have $\log_1(2^k) = k\log 2$. For $i \ge 2$,

$$\log_i(2^k) = \log_{i-1}\!\bigl(\log(2^k)\bigr) = \log_{i-1}(k\log 2).$$

Since each $\log_{i-1}$ is a **slowly varying** function (iterates of $\log$ are slowly varying at infinity), and $k\log 2 \sim k$,

$$\frac{\log_i(2^k)}{\log_{i-1}(k)} \;=\; \frac{\log_{i-1}(k\log 2)}{\log_{i-1}(k)} \;\longrightarrow\; 1 \qquad (k\to\infty).$$

Therefore, for some constant $C > 0$,

$$2^k f(2^k) \;\sim\; \frac{C}{\,k\,\log_1 k\,\log_2 k\,\cdots\,\log_{j-1} k\,(\log_j k)^p\,}.$$

The right-hand side is (a constant multiple of) the general term of $S_{j-1}(p)$. Since the terms are positive and the ratio tends to $1$, the condensed series converges iff $S_{j-1}(p)$ converges. By the induction hypothesis, $S_{j-1}(p)$ converges iff $p > 1$.

By the condensation test, $S_j(p)$ converges iff the condensed series converges, iff $S_{j-1}(p)$ converges, iff $p > 1$. ✓

---

**Conclusion.** By induction on $j$, for every $j \ge 0$ the series

$$\sum_{n=N}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n\,\log n\,\log\log n\,\cdots\,\log_j n\,(\log_{j+1} n)^p}$$

converges if and only if $\boxed{p > 1}$, and diverges for $p \le 1$.
